amiakhum-waterfall.desc: Amiakhum lies in the Nakshiyang area of Thanchi, deep in the hills near the Myanmar border. 'Khum' in Marma means a deep pool that never dries, and here a broad curtain of water falls into one. Getting there takes a tough trek of a day or more beyond Thanchi, often through Bawm and Tripura villages and over steep, muddy slopes. Many trekkers consider it the most beautiful waterfall in Bangladesh, and nearby spots like Satbhaikhum and Velakhum are seen on the same trip.
blocks: How to get there
Jeep from Bandarban town to Thanchi, register and hire a licensed guide, then go by boat and on foot over at least two days.
Good to know

This route lies outside the areas reopened to tourists in 2025, so it may still be closed; check with the Bandarban district administration first. Only go with experienced guides and avoid heavy rain.

glance: 330 km to Bandarban by road, 8–11 hours by bus or car
rijuk-waterfall.desc: Rijuk falls from a cliff right into the Sangu River in Ruma upazila, so you see it from the water. Boats run downstream or upstream along the Sangu from Ruma bazar, passing Marma villages and steep forested banks. The fall runs all year but is fullest in the rainy season. It is less visited than Boga Lake and makes a gentle half-day boat trip.
blocks: How to get there
Jeep from Bandarban town to Ruma, register and hire a licensed guide, then take a boat on the Sangu to the falls.
Good to know
Ruma has had long tourist bans; check whether Rijuk is on the currently permitted route before going. Wear a life jacket on the boat.

glance: 330 km to Bandarban by road, 8–11 hours by bus or car
keokradong.desc: Keokradong in Ruma upazila rises to roughly 986 m and for years was thought to be the country's highest point; later surveys showed other peaks are higher. It is still a classic trek: from Ruma, walkers go via Boga Lake and the Bawm village of Darjeeling Para to the summit, where a small army marker and shelter stand. On clear days the view stretches over wave after wave of hills toward Myanmar and India. It is often wrapped in cloud, especially in the rainy season.
blocks: How to get there
Jeep from Bandarban town to Ruma, register with the authorities and hire a licensed guide, then go via Boga Lake by jeep or on foot and trek to the summit.
Good to know

Tourist access to Ruma and the routes beyond Boga Lake has been closed or limited for security reasons since 2022; when Ruma reopened in 2025 only certain spots were allowed. Check current district administration notices before planning. Carry ID and a registered guide.

glance: About 50–120 BDT per dish at local eateries
Re Khyaing restaurant in Ujanipara, Bandarban town, and other Marma-run eateries in Ujanipara and Madhyampara
bandarban-tojah-laksu.desc: A Marma meal is light on oil and heavy on fresh chilli and herbs. Tojah is a plate of blanched vegetables like cucumber, cabbage and yardlong beans eaten with a sharp chilli and shrimp-paste dip. Laksu is shredded chicken pounded with raw hill chillies, garlic and onion. Both are eaten with plain rice or binni (sticky) rice, often with stir-fried bamboo shoot in the rainy months.

glance: 330 km to Bandarban by road, 8–11 hours by bus or car
debotakhum.desc: Debotakhum is a deep pool in a stream winding through a canyon-like cleft in the hills. The walls rise steeply on both sides and the light filters in from above, giving the water a deep green colour. Visitors paddle in on bamboo rafts or kayaks hired from nearby villages. The trek in passes through jhum fields and small paras.
blocks: How to get there
From Bandarban town go to Rowangchhari, register with authorities, hire a guide and continue to Kochchopotoli, then trek to the khum.
Good to know
Life jackets are essential; the water is deep. Rowangchhari has had periodic tourist bans, so check current advisories. Avoid after heavy rain.

glance: Marma-run eateries in Ujanipara, Bandarban town; small jars are sold in Bandarban town bazar
bandarban-nappi.desc: Nappi is made by fermenting small fish or shrimp until it turns into a salty, strong-smelling paste. Marma cooks use only a little at a time, stirred into boiled vegetables, bamboo shoot or chilli chutneys, where it gives a deep savoury taste. It is the backbone of hill cooking in Bandarban rather than a dish on its own, so ask for food made with it.

nafakhum-waterfall.desc: Nafakhum is where the Remakri stream drops over a broad rock ledge, creating one of the biggest waterfalls in the country by volume. Getting there is an adventure: a country-boat ride up the Sangu from Thanchi past stone rapids, then a trek along the riverbank through Marma villages. The falls are at their most powerful in the rainy season, though the journey is safer after it.
blocks: How to get there
Jeep to Thanchi, register and hire a licensed guide, boat up the Sangu to Remakri, then trek a few hours to the falls.
Good to know

Guides and registration are compulsory. Thanchi has been closed to tourists at times for security reasons; check current notices before travelling. The river rises fast after rain, so do not cross streams in a flood.

glance: 330 km to Bandarban by road, 8–11 hours by bus or car
Small entry ticket; separate charges for vehicles
nilgiri-bandarban.desc: Nilgiri sits at roughly 2,000 feet on the winding road from Bandarban town to Thanchi, and is run by the army. On many mornings, especially in the rainy and post-monsoon months, clouds fill the valleys below the viewpoint so the surrounding hills look like islands. On clear days you can see ridge after ridge rolling toward the Myanmar border. The drive up, past Marma and Mro villages, is part of the experience.
blocks: How to get there
About 2 hours by hired jeep ('chander gari') from Bandarban town along the Thanchi road.
Good to know

Arrive early for clouds. Carry your NID/passport; there are army checkpoints on the road. Foreigners need prior permission to travel in the Chittagong Hill Tracts. Check current government advisories before travelling.

glance: 330 km to Bandarban by road, 8–11 hours by bus or car
nilachal-bandarban.desc: Nilachal sits on a hill just outside Bandarban town, making it the easiest high viewpoint to reach. Terraces and benches look over folded green hills and the town below, and on monsoon mornings clouds drift through the valleys. It is a good first stop on arrival, and a relaxed place to watch the light change in the evening.
blocks: How to get there
About 20 minutes by CNG or jeep from Bandarban town.
Good to know
Go for sunset or early morning. Pair with the Golden Temple on the same afternoon.

glance: Roadside fruit bazar on the Bandarban–Chimbuk road and Bandarban town bazar
bandarban-hill-fruits.desc: Bandarban's slopes are covered with small orchards of papaya, banana and mango, and much of the country's hill fruit comes from here. Farmers bring the fruit down to roadside stalls and weekly hill bazars, where it is cheaper and riper than in city markets. Mangoes come in summer, while papaya and banana are found most of the year.

glance: 330 km to Bandarban by road, 8–11 hours by bus or car
boga-lake.desc: Boga Lake lies at around 1,200 feet in Ruma upazila, and its unusual shape and depth have led to theories that it formed in an old crater. Bawm legend tells of a dragon living in a cave on the site. The water is clear and calm, and the small Bawm village on its shore offers simple homestays. It is also the base for treks to Keokradong.
blocks: How to get there
Jeep from Bandarban town to Ruma bazar, register with authorities and hire a licensed guide, then continue by jeep or on foot to the lake.
Good to know

A registered local guide and checkpoint registration are mandatory. Tourist access to Ruma has been suspended at times for security reasons, most recently in 2024; check current district administration and army notices before going. Swimming in the lake is discouraged because it is very deep.

glance: Indigenous restaurants in Bandarban town and homestays in the hills
bandarban-bashkorol.desc: During the rainy season, new bamboo shoots push up across the hills, and indigenous families harvest them young and tender. They are sliced and cooked with dried fish, pork, chicken or simply with chillies and herbs, and have a mild, slightly earthy crunch. Many hill restaurants in Bandarban serve bamboo shoot dishes when they are in season.

glance: 330 km to Bandarban by road, 8–11 hours by bus or car
bandarban-golden-temple.desc: Known to most visitors as the Golden Temple, Buddha Dhatu Jadi stands on a hill at Balaghata, a few kilometres from Bandarban town. Built in a style reminiscent of Myanmar's pagodas, its golden spires and dragon-guarded stairways glow in the afternoon sun. It is an active place of worship for the Marma Buddhist community, so visitors are expected to keep their voices low.
blocks: How to get there
About 15 minutes by CNG from Bandarban town.
Good to know
Visiting hours are limited and can change; check locally. Dress modestly and remove shoes.

glance: Small Marma-run shops in Bandarban town and Ruma/Thanchi bazars
mundi.desc: Mundi is a dish of fresh rice noodles served in a light, sour-spicy broth, often with fish paste, chilli, herbs and crunchy toppings. It reflects the Marma community's links with Burmese food culture, and is eaten through the day at small shops in Bandarban town. It is quick, cheap and very different from mainstream Bengali food.

glance: 330 km to Bandarban by road, 8–11 hours by bus or car
shoilo-propat.desc: Shoilo Propat is a small waterfall on the Bandarban–Thanchi road, a short drive from town. Cold water slides down a rocky slope into pools that are easy to reach by a flight of steps. It is one of the most visited natural spots in Bandarban because it needs no trek. Bawm villagers set up stalls by the road selling handwoven shawls, fruit and local crafts.
blocks: How to get there
About 20–30 minutes by CNG or jeep from Bandarban town on the Chimbuk/Thanchi road; most Nilgiri-bound jeeps stop here.
Good to know
The rocks are slippery; do not climb the fall itself. Water is thin in the dry season.

sangrai-festival.desc: Sangrai is how the Marma community celebrates the turn of the year in mid-April, part of the wider hill new-year season known as Boisabi. The highlight is the water festival, where young men and women gather around decorated stages and splash each other with water as a gesture of cleansing and goodwill. Homes prepare special cakes and dishes, Buddha images are bathed, and elders are honoured. Bandarban town hosts the largest celebrations.
blocks: Good to know
Join in only where invited, and ask before taking photos of people.
